caber.name: Tossing the caber
caber.rules: A caber is a tapered log, often five metres or more long. You run with it upright, then heave it so it turns end over end. Nobody measures how far. The judge looks at where it lands compared with a clock face with you at six: straight out in front at twelve o'clock is perfect. Hold Confirm to build your run-up and let go in the gold. Too early is a flop, too late is a drop.

plaque.title: The Caber
plaque.text: Caber tossing is judged on the turn, not the distance. A perfect toss lands straight out from the thrower at twelve o'clock. It is the heavy event at Highland gatherings from Braemar to Oban.

caber.won: Twelve o'clock, near enough. The judge nods, which for a caber judge is a standing ovation.

tug.name: Tug of war
tug.rules: Tug of war is a team of eight against a team of eight and a very long argument. Today it is you, your lead creature and a rope. Tap Confirm in time with the beat to heave. A strong creature pulls harder on every good tap, and the other side never stops pulling. Drag the marker over your line before the whistle.

plaque.title: Tug of War
plaque.text: Tug of war was an Olympic event from 1900 to 1920. It is still a fixture at Highland games, where the anchor man digs in his heels and prays to the God of Boots.

tug.won: Over the line! Your creature looks very pleased with itself, and a little bit like it wants to be a team of eight.

hurling.name: Hurling
hurling.rules: Five frees at goal with the sliotar and the hurley. Under the crossbar and past the keeper is a goal, worth three. Over the bar between the posts is a point, worth one. Wide is nothing. The marker drifts around the goal: press Confirm to strike. The keeper leans before he dives, and he is not always honest. Get five points' worth and you've done well.

plaque.title: Hurling
plaque.text: Hurling is among the fastest field games in the world and is said to be about three thousand years old in Ireland. The ball is the sliotar, the stick the hurley. The GAA was founded in Thurles in 1884.

hurling.won: Five points' worth and a clean ball. Cork will talk about it until the next time.

shinty.name: Shinty
shinty.rules: Five shots at the goal. Shinty is twelve a side and only goals count: over the bar is nothing, and a goal is called a hail. The marker drifts around the goal: press Confirm to strike with the caman. The keeper leans before he dives, but not always the way he goes. Three hails and you've earned your tea.

plaque.title: Shinty
plaque.text: Shinty is the Gaelic game of the Highlands, played with a caman, twelve a side. The Camanachd Cup has been played for since 1896, and a goal is called a hail.

shinty.won: Three hails! The keeper shakes your hand. It is a bit like being shaken by a gate.
